clue.text: Reading – Amsterdam, perhaps – discussed by these?

definitions.text: Reading – Amsterdam, perhaps – discussed by these?

blocks.note: surface reading: two places, an English town and a Dutch city, as if the clue were about a trip
setter's reading: Reading is something you read, and Amsterdam is a Booker-winning novel by Ian McEwan, so the group meets to talk about it

explanation.walkthrough: Reading and Amsterdam look like a pair of places; in fact 'Reading' is the activity and Amsterdam is Ian McEwan's 1998 novel, the sort of choice a club of readers would discuss.
explanation.definitionFit: Clubs of readers meet regularly to talk over a chosen novel, so a novel like this is exactly what they discuss.

clue.text: Two arts degrees, that's sweet

blocks.note: BA, Bachelor of Arts
the second of the pair

explanation.surface: Someone gloats that collecting two arts degrees feels sweet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sweet' reads as an adjective of satisfaction, but it is a noun for a dessert.
explanation.definitionFit: A rum baba is a small yeast cake soaked in syrup, a classic British pudding or sweet course.

clue.text: Romania, a little country

indicators.note: a little of something is only part of it, so just a portion of the word is wanted

blocks.note: letters two to five of the country name

explanation.surface: Romania is described as a small nation.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue seems to call Romania a little country; instead a different country sits inside its name.
explanation.definitionFit: Oman is a sultanate on the south-east coast of the Arabian Peninsula, a sovereign nation.

clue.text: Initiate violence, toilet bag not prepared

indicators.note: something not prepared is in a disordered state, so these letters need rearranging

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A row breaks out because someone's washbag was not packed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not' looks like part of the indicator, but it is needed as fodder; 'prepared' alone would leave three letters short.
explanation.definitionFit: To start fighting an enemy is to begin violent conflict, a straightforward phrase-for-phrase synonym.

clue.text: Requires bilge, so babbles

indicators.note: babbling is speaking in a jumbled, incoherent rush, so these letters come out in disorder

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Talking rubbish demands that one keeps on chattering.
explanation.walkthrough: Bilge is slang for nonsense, which suits the babbling surface; here it is just letters.
explanation.definitionFit: If a rule compels someone to act, it places a duty on them, which is what requiring means.

clue.text: Important rising star oddly missing football

indicators.note: in a down entry rising means read from the bottom up, so the letters run backwards
with the odd-numbered positions missing, only the even-placed letters are kept

blocks.note: a star is a very important person
letters two, four, six and eight

explanation.surface: A key young talent on the rise is absent from the football team.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rising star' reads as one phrase about a promising player; 'rising' only turns the star round.
explanation.definitionFit: Something on which everything turns is crucial, so the adjective is a close synonym for significant.

clue.text: He's not out of US Cabinet

indicators.note: made of these letters, so the answer is drawn from within the phrase

blocks.note: runs from the end of the first word into the second

explanation.surface: A politician is reported as still being in the American government.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not out' sounds like cricket or a minister keeping their post; here it means not on strike.
explanation.definitionFit: A strikebreaker keeps working during a stoppage, so he refuses to walk out with colleagues; the term is derogatory slang.

clue.text: Natter about vacuous froth, wee time wasted!

definitions.text: Natter about vacuous froth, wee time wasted!

indicators.note: vacuous means empty, so the word loses its contents and keeps only its outside
wasted can mean wrecked or ruined, so these letters are knocked into a new order
to be about something is to be around it, so one piece is placed round another

blocks.note: to natter is to chat
first and last letters
taken as written
T is the standard abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: Someone grumbles that idle chatter about nothing is a waste of time.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue doubles as the definition: gossiping about empty froth while the time drains away is exactly this idiom.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to talk at leisure about trivial matters, which matches a natter over nothing while time slips by.

clue.text: Desirous boy first getting small rest and biscuit

indicators.note: first fixes the order, putting this piece at the front of the next one

blocks.note: B is a common abbreviation for boy
randy is British slang for lustful
S is the abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels
a nap is a short rest

explanation.surface: An eager lad first has a quick lie-down and then a snack.
explanation.walkthrough: Randy is British informal for sexually eager, a sense many American solvers may not expect.
explanation.definitionFit: A brandy snap is a thin, crisp rolled ginger wafer, a British teatime treat classed as a biscuit or cookie.

clue.text: Horrid child is vain? Not half, the French admitted: that's capital

indicators.note: not half means half is cut away, so only the first part of the word survives
to be admitted is to be let inside, so one piece goes into another

blocks.note: a brat is a badly behaved child
taken as written
first half of the word
la is French for 'the' (feminine)

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a nasty child is conceited, and the French reply 'not half', meaning very much so.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not half!' is a British exclamation meaning 'very much', so the surface reads as a reply; in the wordplay it simply halves the following word, and the French article is admitted into the middle.
explanation.definitionFit: Bratislava is the capital city of Slovakia, on the Danube.

clue.text: Soundly defeat a character from Greece

indicators.note: done soundly, the words are judged by their sound rather than their spelling

blocks.note: to defeat is to beat, followed by 'a'

explanation.surface: A team convincingly beats a Greek opponent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Soundly defeat' reads as one phrase for a thrashing; 'soundly' is the signal, and British speakers say the letter name 'bee-ta'.
explanation.definitionFit: Beta is the second letter of the Greek alphabet, so it is one of the written characters used in Greece.

clue.text: '51: Attlee four times suffering rumours

indicators.note: something suffering is in a bad way, knocked out of shape, so these letters are reordered

blocks.note: 51 in Roman numerals: L is 50 and I is 1
taken as written
T for time, four of them

explanation.surface: In 1951 the Labour prime minister Clement Attlee keeps being hit by gossip.
explanation.walkthrough: Clement Attlee was the British prime minister who lost the 1951 election, so the date looks historical; it is really just a Roman numeral.
explanation.definitionFit: Tittle-tattle is idle gossip, the trivial talk that passes around as hearsay.

clue.text: Punch drunk earlier, journalist giving little away

indicators.note: earlier sets the order, so this piece comes before the one it is attached to

blocks.note: tight is informal for drunk
a punch is delivered with a fist
ED, short for editor

explanation.surface: A reporter who was drunk earlier lets nothing slip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Punch drunk' reads as one phrase meaning dazed, but the two words give separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A miserly person is reluctant to spend or part with money, so they hand over almost nothing.

clue.text: Dogs Spooner's given M Eastern culinary staples

indicators.note: Reverend Spooner famously swapped the opening sounds of words, so the starts here are exchanged

blocks.note: dates and grains are Middle Eastern staples; 'date' takes the GR of 'grains'
'grains' takes the D of 'date'

explanation.surface: Dogs are being fed Middle Eastern cooking basics.
explanation.walkthrough: Swap the opening D and GR of the two foods and you say the dog breed.
explanation.definitionFit: The Great Dane is a giant breed of domestic dog, an example of the general category.

clue.text: In remix, bury a vocal that's list of words ...

indicators.note: a remix reworks a recording into a new version, so these letters are reassembled

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A producer hides the singer's track under the mix of a song.
explanation.walkthrough: The music-studio picture hides a plain rearrangement of three words.
explanation.definitionFit: A vocabulary can mean a glossary, a set of terms with meanings, as in a language textbook.

clue.text: Rectangle ... hang on ... maybe bit unclear ... squashed, primarily!

definitions.text: Rectangle ... hang on ... maybe bit unclear ... squashed, primarily!

indicators.note: primarily means in the first place, so each word contributes its opening letter

blocks.note: first letter
first letter
first letter
first letter
first letter
first letter
first letter

explanation.surface: Someone hesitantly describes a shape: a rectangle, or maybe a squashed one.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the wordplay and a description: push a rectangle over sideways and the right angles go, leaving the slanted shape.
explanation.definitionFit: A rhombus is a four-sided figure with equal sides but no right angles, like a square pushed out of true.

clue.text: Pamphlet tersely conveys messages

indicators.note: to convey is to carry, so the phrase carries the word inside it

blocks.note: runs across the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: A leaflet communicates information briefly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Conveys messages' reads as one predicate about the pamphlet, but the verb only signals the concealment.
explanation.definitionFit: Written correspondence sent through the post consists of notes and communications from one person to another.

clue.text: A priest, old-fashioned, got around, moved with the times

indicators.note: to get around something is to surround it, so one piece encloses another

blocks.note: taken as written
dated means out of fashion
P is a dictionary abbreviation for priest

explanation.surface: An old-fashioned cleric got about and modernised his ways.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Got around' sounds like the priest travelling; it tells you the five-letter word wraps the single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Adjusting to new conditions means changing to suit the present, which is keeping pace with modern life.

clue.text: ... crank up Greek character I've seen with intro of drums

definitions.note: a noun here: deviate as a noun means a deviant, an oddball

indicators.note: an intro is the opening, so only the first letter of the word is used
in a down entry up means read from the bottom, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: first letter
eta is the seventh letter of the Greek alphabet
taken as written, without the apostrophe

explanation.surface: Following on from the previous clue, someone turns up a Greek-style tune after a drum intro.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crank up' reads as turning up the volume; 'crank' is the definition and 'up' starts the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A crank is an eccentric person, and the rare noun sense of deviate is someone departing from normal behaviour.

clue.text: Greek and a Scandinavian heading west to W Indies location

indicators.note: in an across entry west is leftward, so the letters run from right to left

blocks.note: GR is the abbreviation for Greek
a Dane is a Scandinavian from Denmark

explanation.surface: A Greek and a Dane set off westwards for the Caribbean.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heading west' reads as a direction of travel towards the Caribbean, which fits the surface neatly.
explanation.definitionFit: Grenada is an island nation in the Caribbean, part of the West Indies, so it is a place there.

clue.text: Wobbly, pudgy, round – Everyman's diet's beginning – let's go

indicators.note: to go round something is to surround it, so one piece encloses the others
the beginning of a word is its first letter, which is all that is kept
something wobbly is unsteady and out of shape, so the letters are shaken into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
the setter Everyman speaking of himself is I
first letter

explanation.surface: The setter, chubby and wobbly, decides it is time to start a diet.
explanation.walkthrough: Setters often refer to themselves by name, so 'Everyman's' stands for I.
explanation.definitionFit: Giddy-up is the call to make a horse move on, an exclamation urging departure much like a rallying shout.

clue.text: Well-aimed dart, very fine to bag five hundred and one: drink?

indicators.note: to bag something is to capture it, so one piece holds another

blocks.note: a double is a dart landing in the outer ring, scoring twice the number
V is the abbreviation for very
fine means OK
D is 500 in Roman numerals
a means one

explanation.surface: A darts player hits a good shot and celebrates at the bar.
explanation.walkthrough: The darts picture leads straight to a pub, and the question mark marks the definition as just one example of a drink.
explanation.definitionFit: A double measure of a spirit is a common bar order, an example of an alcoholic beverage.

clue.text: 'How to catch fish?' 'Attack with dogs'

blocks.note: first meaning: food put on a hook to lure fish
second meaning: to set dogs on a chained animal

explanation.walkthrough: The quote marks dress the two meanings up as a question and reply; the first is a noun, the second a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Anglers lure fish with food on a hook, and bear- or bull-baiting was the old sport of setting dogs on a tethered animal.

clue.text: Horse, bolt

blocks.note: first meaning: a stallion kept for breeding
second meaning: a short metal pin or rivet

explanation.walkthrough: 'Bolt' tempts as the verb a horse might do, running off; it is the noun for a fastener.
explanation.definitionFit: A breeding stallion is called a stud, and a stud is also a projecting metal fastener like a rivet.

clue.text: Curry accompaniment, whichever way you look at it!

indicators.text: whichever way you look at it
indicators.note: if it looks the same from either direction, the word reads identically left to right and right to left

blocks.clueFragment: whichever way you look at it
blocks.note: the word reads the same from left or right

explanation.surface: Someone insists the bread served with a curry is the same however you regard it.
explanation.walkthrough: The exclamation sounds like a judgement on food; it only says the word is the same in both directions.
explanation.definitionFit: Naan is the leavened flatbread baked in a tandoor and eaten alongside Indian dishes.

clue.text: Empty room getting statuary displaying monarch

indicators.note: an empty word has lost its contents, leaving only its outer letters
displaying something means laying it out in a new arrangement, so these letters are reordered

blocks.note: first and last letters
taken as written

explanation.surface: A bare gallery is filled with sculptures of a king or queen.
explanation.walkthrough: Mary Stuart is Mary, Queen of Scots, executed in 1587.
explanation.definitionFit: Mary Stuart reigned as Queen of Scotland from 1542 to 1567, so she was a sovereign ruler.

clue.text: Orders essentially insane physio

indicators.note: the essence of something is its core, so only the central letters are kept

blocks.note: middle two letters
middle two letters

explanation.surface: A deranged physiotherapist issues commands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Orders' looks like a noun, but it is a verb, as in 'Simon says'.
explanation.definitionFit: When someone in authority states what must happen, as in 'the boss says so', they are commanding it.

clue.text: Having gone backward, Spanish car's finally gone forward – fixed!

indicators.note: going backward means travelling in the opposite direction, so the letters run in reverse
finally points to the end, so only each word's last letter is kept

blocks.note: having gone to the toilet, informally
SEAT is a Spanish car maker
last letters of the two words

explanation.surface: A Spanish car that kept rolling backwards finally moves forward, repaired.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fixed' reads as repaired, the end of the car story; here it means firmly established. 'Gone' is the euphemism for a trip to the toilet.
explanation.definitionFit: A deep-seated belief is firmly established and hard to shift, so it is entrenched in the sense of immovable.
